title: Workflows, agents and who owns the control flow

items.stem: Which question best separates a workflow from an agent?

options.text: Does the system call the language model more than once per request?
Does the code or the model choose each next step while it runs?
Does the system use tools such as a calendar or manual search?
Is the model large enough to plan several steps ahead on its own?

items.stem: For every booking request, the makerspace program runs the same steps in code: look up the student's training record, check the calendar, create the booking, and then ask the model to write a confirmation message. The model chooses none of these steps. What is this design?

options.text: An agent, because it books equipment by calling several tools
An agent, because a language model is called as part of it
A workflow, because the code decides the steps and their order
A workflow, because it never calls the model more than once

items.stem: A rule says every booking must check training, check the calendar, book the slot and send a confirmation, in that order, with no exceptions. Why is a fixed workflow the better choice for this part of the assistant?

options.text: The order never varies, so code gets it right every time, with fewer model calls and easier testing
A workflow lets the model skip a step whenever it judges that the step is not needed
An agent cannot call tools in a set order, so only a workflow can follow the rule
A workflow needs no language model at all, so it always costs less than an agent

items.stem: Which of these makerspace tasks is the best candidate for an agent rather than a fixed workflow?

options.text: Sending every student a reminder message 24 hours before their booked slot
Answering "what is the maximum material thickness?" with one manual lookup
Confirming a booking by running the same four checks in the same order
Diagnosing "my 3D print keeps failing", where each result decides what to look up next

items.stem: Your sponsor's budget covers 1,200 model calls. Assume every model call costs the same. A fixed workflow makes exactly 2 model calls per request. An agent averages 6 model calls per request. How many more requests can the budget cover with the workflow than with the agent?
A teammate says, "Our booking flow uses a language model and tools, so it is an agent." In one sentence, what is wrong with that reasoning?
